title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Distributed Serving & Request Routing
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 8)
Understanding Distributed Serving & Request Routing

In the previous parts, we explored tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and data parallelism. At this point, we understand that modern inference systems use many GPUs together to run large models and handle large numbers of users.
But something still feels incomplete.
What actually happens when a request first arrives?
And when we say a request is routed to a “replica,” what exactly does that mean?
What happens when a request first arrives?
Suppose a user sends:
"Explain quantum computing"
At first glance, it feels simple:

request goes to model
model generates response
But internally, many things happen before the first token is generated.
Step 1 — The request reaches the API layer
The request first reaches an API gateway or frontend service.
Example:

User
  ↓
API Gateway
This layer may handle:

authentication
rate limiting
logging
validation
API management
At this stage, the request has still not reached the GPUs.
Step 2 — The router/load balancer receives the request
Next, the request reaches the routing layer.
Example:

Gateway
   ↓
Router / Load Balancer
This component decides:
Which model replica should handle this request?
What is a replica?
This is where things become interesting.
At first, I was thinking about replicas similar to traditional web servers behind a load balancer. In normal applications:

each server has its own IP
the load balancer routes traffic across servers
each server independently processes requests
Example:

Load Balancer
   ↓
Web Server 1
Web Server 2
Web Server 3
But LLM inference systems are different.
A replica is usually not just:

one GPU or even
one server
A replica is actually:
one complete model-serving unit
And that unit itself may contain:

many GPUs
multiple pipeline stages
tensor parallel groups
schedulers
KV cache
communication layers
Can a replica span multiple GPUs?
Yes.
Suppose we have:

tensor parallel size = 4
pipeline parallel size = 4
Then:

4 GPUs per stage
×
4 stages
=
16 GPUs
Now these 16 GPUs together form:
ONE model replica
The request is not independently handled by one GPU.
Instead:

all GPUs cooperate together
tensor parallel GPUs compute the same layer together
pipeline stages process different parts of the model
So the replica behaves like:
one giant distributed inference engine
Does one replica always mean one server?
Not necessarily.
For smaller models:

one replica may fit inside one server
all GPUs may live in the same machine
Example:

Server A
├── GPU 1
├── GPU 2
├── GPU 3
└── GPU 4
In this case:
replica ≈ one server
But for larger models:
one replica may span many servers
Example:

Replica 1
├── Server A → GPUs 1–8
├── Server B → GPUs 9–16
├── Server C → GPUs 17–24
└── Server D → GPUs 25–32
Now:

one replica
spans multiple servers
and many GPUs
How do these servers work together?
The servers are connected using high-speed networking.
Inside one server:

GPUs often communicate using NVLink or NVSwitch
communication is extremely fast
Across servers:

systems may use InfiniBand or RDMA networking
optimized for very high throughput and low latency
This allows:

GPUs across machines
to behave like one coordinated inference system
So a useful way to think about it is:

Replica
=
a distributed cluster of GPUs
acting as one logical model instance
What does the load balancer actually balance then?
The load balancer usually routes traffic across replicas.
Example:

Load Balancer
   ↓
Replica 1 → GPUs 1–16
Replica 2 → GPUs 17–32
Replica 3 → GPUs 33–48
The load balancer is usually not routing directly to individual GPUs.
Instead:

each replica internally coordinates its GPUs
the replica itself behaves like one serving target
How does the router choose a replica?
The router may consider:

current GPU utilization
queue length
KV cache pressure
batch size
latency
memory availability
Example:

Replica 1 → overloaded
Replica 2 → healthy
Replica 3 → long queue
So the router selects:
Replica 2
Why is routing important?
Because inference systems constantly balance:

throughput
vs
latency
If too many requests go to one replica:

queues grow
latency increases
KV cache pressure increases
If requests are spread too aggressively:

GPUs become underutilized
batching efficiency drops
So routing becomes a scheduling problem.
What happens after replica selection?
Once a request reaches a replica:

Request
   ↓
Replica Scheduler
The scheduler decides:

when to execute the request
which batch it should join
whether enough memory is available
This is where continuous batching becomes important.
Why don’t requests execute immediately?
Because GPUs are more efficient with batches.
Instead of:

1 request
→ 1 GPU execution
the scheduler tries to create:
Batch = [Request A, Request B, Request C]
Now the GPUs process them together.
What happens during prefill?
The prompt tokens are first processed through the transformer layers.
Example:
"Explain quantum computing"
becomes token IDs like:
During this stage:

attention is computed
activations flow through layers
KV cache gets created
This phase is called: Prefill
What happens during decode?
Once KV cache exists:

token generation starts
one token depends on previous tokens
Example:

Token 1
→ Token 2
→ Token 3
This phase becomes sequential.
This is called the decode loop.
Why do requests usually stay on the same replica?
Because the KV cache already exists there.
Example:

User Session
   ↓
Replica 2
   ↓
KV cache stored there
If generation suddenly moves to another replica:

KV cache would need transfer
latency would increase heavily
bandwidth usage would explode
This is why systems often use:

sticky sessions
or
session affinity
What is the overall request flow?
At a high level:

User
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Router / Load Balancer
 ↓
Replica
 ↓
Scheduler
 ↓
Batch Formation
 ↓
Prefill
 ↓
Decode Loop
 ↓
Generated Tokens
This is the basic lifecycle of a request inside a modern inference system.
What still feels unclear at this point?
Honestly, while learning this myself, one thing initially confused me:

what exactly is a replica physically?
where are the GPUs located?
how do multiple servers behave like one system?
how does GPU communication actually work underneath?
At this stage, it is completely normal for these questions to appear.
Because now we are slowly transitioning from:

“running a model on GPUs” to
“understanding distributed GPU infrastructure”
And that is a very different mental model.
What comes next?
Now that we understand:

request routing
replicas
schedulers
session affinity
distributed model serving
the next natural step becomes:

How do all these GPUs and servers
actually communicate fast enough
to behave like ONE system?
In the next part, we will go deeper into:

GPU clusters
NVLink
NVSwitch
InfiniBand
inter-node communication
why networking becomes critical
and what “inside a replica” really looks like.
This is where inference systems start looking much closer to distributed supercomputing systems than traditional backend applications.
